generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport a reference list is read closely. It shows whether you have engaged with the key studies, the recent work and the dissenting voices, so it signals the scope of your reading. How you use those sources shows your critical edge: whether you simply cite an influential finding or set it against a study that failed to replicate, or against what coaches observe in training. A marker reading your citations is reading how you think about evidence, not only checking that you have not copied.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students submit essays on a training method that both avoid plagiarism and both reference correctly.

Tom cites a source after almost every sentence, each one a well-known coaching researcher, each dropped in to back a point already made. The citations are accurate and the list is long. But they all pull the same way: no finding is set against another, so the reader sees reading, not thinking. The references prove Tom did the reading, and little more.

Amara cites fewer sources but uses them against one another: one study supporting the method is introduced, then qualified by a later one that failed to replicate it, and the paragraph reaches a position of its own. The same conventions now carry a visibly critical argument. The reader can see Amara weighing the evidence, not just reporting it.

Both reference correctly. Only Amara made the references work as evidence of thinking, which is what they are for.
generatedProse.summary: Referencing in the School of Sport does far more than keep you clear of plagiarism. It credits the researchers and coaches you build on and lets others credit you, so the field's conversation can accumulate. It also signals the scope of your reading and the critical edge of your thinking, such as weighing a training study against one that failed to replicate. You can now justify referencing as joining a conversation, explain what references tell a reader, and defend referencing on grounds stronger than fear of a penalty. The last lesson turns to the judgement involved in using sources well.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara's references show a stronger critical edge than Tom's?

items.text: She set studies against one another, such as a finding against a failed replication, to reach a position.
She cited far more studies than Tom did.
She placed a citation after almost every sentence.
She chose more famous researchers than Tom did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Setting studies against one another, rather than stacking agreement, is the critical edge a reader can see.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what Amara did with the studies, not how many there were.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The critical edge came from setting studies against one another to reach a position. Citing more, citing after every sentence, or citing famous names does not show thinking by itself.
